newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Deal on infotech trade within reach at WTO meet.
newsitem.headline: Deal on infotech trade within reach at WTO meet.

text.p: A deal to liberalise trade in the world's $600 billion market for information technology was within grasp on Tuesday after a day of intense haggling, ministers and officials said.

Senior trade officials from the United States, European Union and Japan held a flurry of negotiations throughout the day in an effort to resolve differences on an Information Technology Agreement (ITA) they hope will crown the first ministerial meeting of the fledgling World Trade Organisation (WTO).

The big trading powers made good progress narrowing their differences Tuesday on the types of products to be covered and timing of tariff reductions, but officials said some details remained to be worked out.
At the same time, the United States, European Union and Japan were redoubling efforts to sell the idea to their Asian trading partners.

"We are making a lot of progress and we hope to make further progress this afternoon," European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said after a luncheon with ministers from the United States, Japan and Canada.

Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefksy said she concurred with Brittan's comments, but declined to say anything more on the proposed pact to eliminate tariffs on an estimated A$600 billion of computer and telecommunications products by 2000.
Canadian Trade Minister Art Eggleton expressed optimism about a deal by Friday despite objections from some countries like Malaysia to the ITA negotiations being carried out in Singapore.
"Nothing's for sure until we finish the negotiations, but it's certainly moving in a very positive direction right now," Eggleton said.

Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told the second day of the Conference he hoped "ardently....that we will have an agreement as the most significant achievement of this ministerial conference in the area of trade liberalisation."
However, several Asian nations have voiced reservations, with Malaysia saying the goal of free commerce in infotech by the turn of the century is too ambitious.
Malaysia opposed negotiating the pact and said it did not see agreement by the close of this week's meeting on Friday.
"We did not come here to discuss the Information Technology Agreement," international trade and industry minister Rafidah Aziz said. "All negotiations should be done in Geneva."

But U.S. officials, who have been pushing the ITA hard with the backing of Japan, hope a deal here will build momentum for further trade liberalisation and spur negotiations on another agreement to open up basic telephone services markets.

"There is no question that what the industrialised countries now hope for most here is a deal on information technology products and agreement to work hard for a basic telecommunications pact by February," said one key negotiator.

The 128 full delegations from WTO member countries and ministers and officials from nearly 30 others waiting to be admitted to the organisation have heard ringing appeals for progress to a telecoms liberalisation pact.

Negotiators at WTO headquarters in Geneva are facing a deadline to finalise a deal among some 50 countries by mid-February after failing in an earlier bid last April when the United States pulled out of the talks.
This sector, heavily protected in many emerging economies, is estimated to be worth well over $500 billion annually.

As the full conference entered its second day on Tuesday, key ministers and their aides from different areas of the globe met in conclave to try to hammer out the final text of a declaration to be issued at the end of the gathering on Friday.

Sixteen of 20 paragraphs have been agreed, but there was no doubt a major battle was under way over the last four -- touching mainly on the "new issues" such as labour standards, corruption in trade and competition and investment that have proved the most divisive in Singapore.

Officials said negotiating on whether the declaration, meant to point the WTO down the free trade path into the 21st century, should include any reference at all to the labour issue was being left to last.
